issues.legal_issue: A decision of a High Court on an appeal from a statutory arbitrator’s award remains an arbitral award and is not appealable as an ordinary court judgment, decree, or order.
material_facts: The dispute concerned compensation for property requisitioned by the Government, and the amount was referred by statute to an arbitrator because the parties had not agreed on compensation.
The arbitrator made an award, and a party appealed that award to the High Court under the same statutory scheme.

The statute described the arbitrator’s decision as an award and provided an appeal to the High Court; the proceedings originated as arbitration rather than as a civil suit heard by the High Court in its ordinary jurisdiction.
The High Court modified the award, and both parties obtained certificates to appeal further under the ordinary civil procedure provisions.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s decision was an award, not a judgment, decree, or order appealable under the ordinary civil procedure provisions or the relevant Letters Patent. Both appeals were incompetent and were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A decision made by a court in its ordinary civil jurisdiction is generally appealable under the Code of Civil Procedure, but an adjudication of an arbitrator that receives the court’s imprimatur is final, subject to the applicable statutory provisions. The same distinction applies to statutory arbitration: a reference to a court as a court ordinarily attracts its usual procedures and appeal rights, whereas a reference to it as an arbitrator or designated authority produces an award. An appeal from an award continues the original arbitration proceedings and does not change their character. The Court applied the principles in Rangoon Botatoung Company v. The Collector, Rangoon; The Special Officer, Salsette Building Sites v. Dossabhai Bezonji; The Special Officer, Salsette Building Sites v. Dassabhai Bozanji Motiwala; Manavikraman Tirumalpad v. The Collector of the Nilgiris; Secretary of State for India in Council v. Hindusthan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd.; and Kollegal Silk Filatures Ltd. v. Province of Madras. It distinguished National Telephone Company Ltd. v. Postmaster-General, where the reference was to a tribunal as a court. The relevant statutory framework included sections 19(1)(b), 19(1)(f), and 19(1)(g) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, and sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.statutory_appeal_from_arbitrator_award: A party brought a statutory appeal to a High Court from an arbitrator’s award.
predicates.compensation_referred_to_arbitrator: A statute assigned the determination of compensation to an arbitrator because the parties did not agree on the amount.
predicates.arbitrator_decision_designated_as_award: The governing statutory scheme described the arbitrator’s decision as an award.

issues.definition: When a statutory appeal concerns an award made after compensation was referred to an arbitrator, and the governing scheme designates that decision as an award, an ordinary further appeal is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: Leave to appeal under an inherited jurisdiction limited to appeals from judgments in civil cases cannot be granted against a High Court decision that is an arbitral award rather than a judgment.
material_facts: The parties sought to rely on a power said to have passed from the Privy Council to the Federal Court and then to the Supreme Court to grant leave to appeal.
The challenged High Court decision arose from an appeal against an arbitrator’s award and was held not to be a judgment, decree, or order of the High Court.
The asserted power to grant leave was limited to a proposed appeal against a judgment of a High Court in a civil case.
issues.conclusion: The asserted inherited jurisdiction did not permit leave to appeal because the challenged decision was an award, not a qualifying judgment. No order granting leave could have been made under that power.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(a)(ii) of the Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948, the Federal Court’s power to grant leave applied only where the proposed appeal was against a judgment; section 2(b) defined the relevant judgment as a judgment, decree, or order of a High Court in a civil case. The Court held that Article 135 of the Constitution did not enlarge that power to cover an arbitral award that was not such a judgment.

predicates.special_leave_sought: A party sought special leave to appeal under a jurisdiction asserted to have been inherited from an earlier appellate court.
predicates.impugned_decision_was_arbitral_award: The challenged decision was an arbitral award rather than a judgment, decree, or order of a High Court in a civil case.
predicates.inherited_leave_power_limited_to_civil_j: The asserted inherited power permitted leave only for an appeal from a High Court judgment in a civil case.

issues.definition: If special leave is sought under an inherited power limited to civil judgments and the challenged decision is an arbitral award, leave under that power is unavailable.
